descriptor: A solitary, hook-lipped browser of the African bush, slowly recovering after poachers killed nearly all of its kind.

physical.fact: Its pointed upper lip is prehensile, letting it grip and strip leaves and twigs from shrubs.

range.summary: Guarded parks, conservancies and fenced sanctuaries across eastern and southern Africa, with most animals in South Africa, Namibia, Kenya and Zimbabwe.

regions.name: Kunene and Etosha
regions.note: Desert-adapted black rhinos roam unfenced communal land in Namibia's Kunene region.

regions.name: KwaZulu-Natal parks
regions.note: Zululand reserves kept black rhinos and sent 20 to restock Kruger, where they had died out, in 1971.

regions.name: Laikipia and Tsavo
regions.note: Kenya conserves about 75% of all eastern black rhinos, mostly in guarded sanctuaries.

regions.name: Zimbabwe Lowveld
regions.note: Lowveld conservancies such as Save Valley and Bubye Valley hold most of Zimbabwe's black rhinos.

regions.name: Zakouma, Chad
regions.note: The last black rhino in Chad was recorded in Zakouma in 1972.

regions.name: Northern Cameroon
regions.note: Surveys in 2006 found no sign; the western black rhino was declared extinct in 2011.

regions.name: Mwabvi, Malawi
regions.note: Malawi's last native black rhinos left signs at Mwabvi in 1989; the species was declared extinct in 1990.

regions.name: Liwonde, Malawi
regions.note: Two black rhinos from Kruger brought the species back to Malawi at Liwonde in 1993.

regions.name: South Luangwa, Zambia
regions.note: Heavy poaching in the 1980s emptied the Luangwa Valley; Zambia declared them extinct in 1998.

regions.name: North Luangwa, Zambia
regions.note: Five black rhinos from South Africa returned the species to Zambia at North Luangwa in 2003.

regions.name: Rwanda
regions.note: Poachers wiped out the last black rhinos in Akagera; the final confirmed sighting was in 2007.

regions.name: Akagera return
regions.note: 18 eastern black rhinos from South Africa were reintroduced to Akagera in 2017, ten years on.

rangeHistory.note: Where rhinos were lost and later returned, the loss and the reintroduction are shown as two nearby markers.

population.unit: wild black rhinos in Africa (continental estimate)

source.label: IUCN SSC African Rhino Specialist Group, via IUCN

population.note: The 1960 and 1973 figures are back-estimates quoted in the 2020 Red List assessment. Later points are year-end AfRSG estimates; revised figures put the mid-1990s low near 2,354.

threats.title: Poaching for horn
threats.detail: Organised networks kill rhinos to supply carved and medicinal horn markets in Asia.

threats.title: Rising protection costs
threats.detail: Heavy security spending has led some private owners to give up their rhinos, shrinking safe range.

threats.title: Small, isolated populations
threats.detail: Most rhinos live in separate sanctuaries, so growth depends on careful translocation between them.

threats.title: Habitat loss
threats.detail: Farming and settlement have taken over most of the species' former range across Africa.

places.name: Etosha National Park
places.note: Floodlit waterholes at Okaukuejo draw black rhinos after dark.

places.name: Kunene region
places.note: Desert-adapted rhinos tracked on foot with community rhino rangers.

places.name: Hluhluwe-iMfolozi Park
places.note: The park whose rhinos seeded populations across southern Africa.

places.name: Ol Pejeta Conservancy
places.note: The largest black rhino sanctuary in East Africa.

places.name: Ngorongoro Crater
places.note: A small population often seen on the open crater floor.

sightings.tip: The dry season thins the bush and pulls rhinos to water, making them far easier to find. Black rhinos are shy, so patience at waterholes pays.

actions.title: Never buy rhino horn
actions.detail: Horn is made of keratin, like fingernails, and every purchase funds poaching.

actions.title: Fund rangers and monitoring
actions.detail: Well-equipped rangers and tracking teams are the front line against poachers.

actions.title: Visit community conservancies
actions.detail: Tourism income gives local people a direct stake in keeping rhinos alive.

actions.title: Report wildlife crime
actions.detail: Pass tips about horn trafficking to TRAFFIC or local authorities.

summary.text: The black rhinoceros, also called the black rhino or the hooked-lip rhinoceros, is a species of rhinoceros native to East and Southern Africa, including Angola, Botswana, Eswatini, Kenya, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Tanzania, Zambia, and Zimbabwe. Although the species is referred to as black, its colours vary from brown to grey. It is the only extant species of the genus Diceros.
